clue.text: Clumsy ape squeezing mine hard — something to remember me by?

indicators.note: to squeeze something is to hold it tightly inside, so one piece wraps round another
something clumsy is awkwardly put together, so these letters come out in a muddled order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a pit is a coal mine
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A clumsy ape gets a grip on someone's mine and leaves a memento.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures someone asking to be remembered; the question mark marks the definition as a description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitaph is the inscription on a tomb, words by which the dead person is remembered.

clue.text: The ones vulgarly after sex product

indicators.note: one piece placed after another means they are joined in that order

parts.note: IT is slang for sex, as in 'doing it'
'em is the casual, clipped form of them, the ones

explanation.surface: A smutty remark about whatever turns up after sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vulgarly' signals the dropped-letter slang form of 'them'.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is a single article or product for sale, as in an item of stock.

clue.text: In short, Brian and Brenda's supplementary tipple

indicators.note: in short asks for an abbreviated form of a name rather than the whole of it

parts.note: Private Eye calls Prince Charles 'Brian'; Chas is the short form of Charles
Private Eye calls the Queen 'Brenda'; ER is her royal cipher (Elizabeth Regina)

explanation.surface: Charles and his mother sharing an extra drink, Private Eye style.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's nicknames: Brian for Prince Charles, Brenda for the Queen. Shortened Charles is CHAS, and the Queen is ER.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaser is a drink taken straight after another, such as a beer after a whisky.

clue.text: Has no goolies (neck's present)

indicators.note: something present is there already in the words, waiting to be read across their join

parts.note: read straight across the end of the first word and into the next two

explanation.surface: A rude jibe at some man's manhood, with a remark about a neck tacked on.
explanation.definitionFit: To neck is slang for kissing passionately, the same activity as a snog.

clue.text: Bollocks lacking? Sensible

parts.note: lacking something means having no amount of it
bollocks is British slang for nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a man lacks testicles, then praises his good sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bollocks lacking' becomes the phrase 'no nonsense', with the lack read first.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-nonsense person is practical and down-to-earth, which is sensible.

clue.text: Piss off like an idiot attending Open University

indicators.note: attending means going along with, so one piece stands next to the other

parts.note: screwy means crazy or idiotic
the usual abbreviation of Britain's distance-learning university

explanation.surface: A rude dismissal aimed at a dim student of the Open University.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are coarse exclamations telling someone to go away.

clue.text: Balls placed over doctor's big instrument

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece placed over another sits first, above the next one

parts.note: balls and bull are both slang for nonsense
to doctor accounts is to fiddle or falsify them

explanation.surface: A smutty boast about a doctor's large equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: A bull fiddle is an American name for the double bass, the largest of the violin family.

clue.text: Maybe a baron's "bought it"?

parts.note: surface reading: a baron has died, since 'bought it' is slang for being killed
setter's reading: a baron's title may have been literally purchased, a dig at honours for cash

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks invite the slang sense of dying, but the joke is about titles sold to party donors.
explanation.definitionFit: A baron holds the lowest rank of the nobility, and that rank is a type of peerage.

clue.text: Nit screwed up, entering ground zero attack

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so this piece sits within the others

parts.note: a pitch is a sports ground
O looks like the figure zero

indicators.note: something screwed up is crumpled or botched, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: An idiot blunders into the site of a nuclear blast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground zero' looks like one phrase but splits into two pieces, with the jumbled letters going in between.
explanation.definitionFit: To pitch into someone is an idiom for launching a vigorous attack on them.

clue.text: Offensive from Conservative blue

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
blue jokes are rude, smutty ones

explanation.surface: An offensive remark from a Tory, whose party colour is blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the Conservative colour, which hides its sense of smutty.
explanation.definitionFit: Crude language is vulgar and likely to cause offence.

clue.text: "X" part of the Dirty Digger's empire

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the multiplication sign is read as '...'

definitions.text: part of the Dirty Digger's empire
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the London newspaper owned by Rupert Murdoch, whom Private Eye calls the Dirty Digger

explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye nicknames the Australian-born Rupert Murdoch the Dirty Digger; digger is slang for an Australian.
explanation.definitionFit: X is the arithmetic symbol spoken as 'times', and The Times is a newspaper in Murdoch's group.

clue.text: Creep getting, pervertedly, leg over left and right

indicators.note: pervertedly means in a twisted way, so the letters are bent out of their order

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A creep getting his leg over, kinkily, left and right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leg over' is British slang for sex, which makes it a natural-looking phrase to hide fodder in.
explanation.definitionFit: A creep is a fawning sycophant, someone who grovels to superiors.

clue.text: Local dish excited over massive grope? "Not I"

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: excited means worked up

indicators.note: not I tells us to drop that single letter from the phrase before it

parts.note: massive is big, and a grope is a rub

explanation.surface: A dish at the local leads to an eager, enormous grope, which someone disowns.
explanation.walkthrough: The local is the British word for one's regular pub, and pub grub is the food served there.
explanation.definitionFit: Pub grub is the plain food served in a pub, the dishes of a British local.

clue.text: Sixties feminists' suggestion to their sisters, on catching Sun editor pissed?

indicators.note: catching means seizing and holding, so one piece holds the other inside it

parts.words: Sixties feminists' suggestion to their sisters
parts.note: bra-burning sixties feminists urged women to get their bras off
S is the abbreviation for Sun
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: Sixties feminists spot a drunk tabloid editor and urge each other to strip.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid. 'Pissed' looks like drunk, but here it is the American sense of annoyed, as in pissed off.
explanation.definitionFit: Brassed off is British slang for fed up or annoyed, the American sense of pissed.

clue.text: Good bloke, shagger, one producing a course?

parts.note: a brick is an old-fashioned word for a reliable, decent person
a layer is one who lays, slang for has sex with

explanation.surface: A decent fellow who sleeps around is praised as a chef producing a course of a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests a meal, but here it is a row of bricks in a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A bricklayer builds walls course by course, each course being one horizontal row of bricks.

clue.text: Cambridge lot bound to accept tip from Hillary?

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a bound is a spring or leap

indicators.note: a tip is an extreme end, here the far end of the name that follows

parts.note: the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: A Cambridge group is set to take advice from Hillary Clinton.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cambridge Five were Soviet spies recruited at Cambridge University. Here the tip is the end of the name, not its start.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cambridge spies, such as Philby and Burgess, formed the most famous British spy ring.

clue.text: What some politicians are coy to reveal in full — like the queen (a bad sign) having amusing day?

definitions.text: What some politicians are coy to reveal in full

indicators.note: having means holding, so the jumbled letters hold the next piece inside them
bad letters are spoilt, so they come out in the wrong order

parts.note: camp means flamboyantly effeminate, as a stereotypical queen is
taken as written, then jumbled with the next word
taken as written, then jumbled
fun as an adjective means amusing
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A camp politician has a fun day out while hiding something from the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The queen' is the slang term for an effeminate gay man, not the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Campaign funds are donations for electioneering, whose full sources politicians are often reluctant to disclose.

clue.text: Expecting Labour to follow eventually

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a description of a state that ends in childbirth

explanation.walkthrough: Capital L Labour suggests the political party following on, but it is the labour of childbirth.
explanation.definitionFit: A pregnant woman is said to be expecting, and labour is the birth that eventually ends a pregnancy.

clue.text: In the sack, holding mad Tory, getting end away — climax not reached

indicators.note: holding means keeping inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: in the sack is slang for in bed, so abed

indicators.note: mad means deranged, so the letters are thrown into disorder
getting the end away means losing the last letter of the word

parts.note: taken as written, then cut and jumbled

explanation.surface: A sexual encounter in bed with a crazed Conservative that ends unsatisfyingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting his end away' is British slang for having sex, which disguises the instruction to drop the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something aborted was stopped before completion, never reaching its intended culmination.

clue.text: Ex-PM starts to eliminate 'negative' unbeliever

parts.note: Edward Heath was British Prime Minister in the 1970s

indicators.note: starts are opening letters, so each of the next two words gives its first

parts.note: the opening letter of each word

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister sets out to get rid of anything negative.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen is someone who does not believe in the prevailing religion, an unbeliever.

clue.text: Evidence of awful BSE climax

indicators.note: awful means dreadful, so the letters come out in a dreadful mess

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled
a climax is a peak

explanation.surface: Signs of mad cow disease reaching its terrible height.
explanation.walkthrough: BSE is bovine spongiform encephalopathy, the British 'mad cow' epidemic of the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: To bespeak something is to indicate or give evidence of it, as manners bespeak good breeding.

clue.text: Shit lover once on holiday island

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
Crete is a popular Greek holiday island

explanation.surface: Someone calls their old flame a shit while sunning themselves on a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shit' reads as an insult for the lover, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To excrete is to discharge waste from the body, which is what the verb shit means crudely.

clue.text: "We want a bung from you", said to be an element of candidate selection in US

definitions.text: an element of candidate selection in US

indicators.note: said means spoken, so we want a word that sounds like the request

parts.note: a bung is a stopper or cork, so the request is to cork us

explanation.surface: A demand for a bribe, a bung in British slang, during American party politics.
explanation.walkthrough: A bung is British slang for a bribe, which fits the political surface, but here it is a stopper.
explanation.definitionFit: A caucus is a meeting of party members in some US states to choose their candidates.

clue.text: Ranted about Brown getting in: "Not working"

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so this piece goes inside the other
about means round and round, so the letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled
dun is a dull greyish-brown colour

explanation.surface: Someone rants about Gordon Brown entering Number 10, saying it isn't working.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on Brown points to the former Prime Minister; it is only a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone made redundant has lost their job, so is out of work.

clue.text: see 27dn
Middle of Sun has taboo word: name moved two the left, so not censored

indicators.note: the middle of a short word is its central letter

parts.note: the central letter of the three

indicators.note: shifting the letter for name two places leftward rearranges the word's order

parts.note: the most taboo of English swear words

explanation.surface: The Sun newspaper prints a forbidden word in full.
explanation.walkthrough: N is the abbreviation for name; moving it two places left inside the taboo word turns C-U-N-T into N-C-U-T.
explanation.definitionFit: An uncut film or text has had nothing removed, so it has not been censored.

clue.text: ( + 25dn.) VD? Put gin on balls

indicators.note: put on means placed next to, so the two pieces are set end to end

parts.note: the clap is slang for gonorrhoea, a venereal disease
a gin is a snare or trap

explanation.surface: Venereal disease and gin applied to one's testicles: a grim picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gin' suggests the drink but is a trap, and 'balls' is slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Claptrap is empty, pretentious nonsense, which is what balls means as slang.

clue.text: Slight, sad life, Gordon, ultimately

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of the name just before it

parts.note: the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: A sad, insignificant life for Gordon Brown in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Elfin describes someone small and delicate, of slight build like an elf.

clue.text: Point by Jack, spinning actual "end of sleaze"? Come!

parts.note: E is a compass point, east

indicators.note: spinning means whirling about, so the letters are whirled into a new order

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards
taken as written, then jumbled

indicators.note: end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A commentator on political sleaze points at Jack and urges him on.
